findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

findings.description: 20 fiber pairs analysed. Mean MCD 58 microseconds (reference <35). Increased jitter in 14 of 20 pairs (70%); impulse blocking in 20% of pairs.
findings.muscle: Left orbicularis oculi (voluntary activation, concentric needle)

output.impression: Abnormal single-fiber EMG of the left orbicularis oculi: markedly increased jitter (mean MCD 58 microseconds) with impulse blocking, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description: MRD1 0.5 mm before; ice pack over the closed lid for 2 minutes; MRD1 3.0 mm immediately after (improvement 2.5 mm).
MRD1 2.5 mm before; 4.0 mm after (improvement 1.5 mm).

output.impression: Positive ice pack test: left MRD1 improved by 2.5 mm after 2 minutes of cooling (positive threshold 2 mm); right MRD1 improved by 1.5 mm.
FVC 3.35 L (86% predicted, 47 mL/kg), MIP -70 cmH2O and MEP 92 cmH2O within reference limits; effective cough. Normal respiratory muscle function at this time.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 11.2 nmol/L with elevated blocking antibody; MuSK negative; TSH and free T4 normal
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable ptosis with dysarthria and dysphagia worse in the evening: AChR binding antibody is the first-line serological test and TSH screens for coexisting autoimmune thyroid disease (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025; Evoli A et al., Neurol Sci 2019).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 12-16% in anconeus, trapezius and orbicularis oculi; normal CMAPs, no facilitation, normal NCS and needle EMG
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz including facial and proximal muscles
action_criteria.rationale: RNS of clinically weak facial and proximal muscles confirms the neuromuscular transmission defect; nerve conduction and needle EMG in the same study address diabetic neuropathy and motor neuron disease as alternatives (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left MRD1 improved from 0.5 mm to 3.0 mm after 2 minutes of ice
action_criteria.label: Perform the ice pack test on the more ptotic left eyelid
action_criteria.rationale: Bilateral asymmetric ptosis: an MRD1 improvement of at least 2 mm after 2-5 minutes of cooling supports a neuromuscular transmission disorder at the bedside.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No anterior mediastinal mass; age-appropriate fatty thymic involution
action_criteria.label: Order mediastinal CT with contrast to look for thymoma
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with MG; a thymoma would indicate thymectomy regardless of age (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 86% predicted (47 mL/kg), MIP -70 and MEP 92 cmH2O, effective cough
action_criteria.label: Measure baseline respiratory function (FVC, MIP, MEP)
action_criteria.rationale: Progressive bulbar weakness with dysphagia to liquids: baseline FVC, MIP and MEP stage the respiratory risk and serve as the reference for serial measurement if he worsens (Lawn ND et al., Arch Neurol 2001).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Increased jitter with blocking in orbicularis oculi
action_criteria.label: Single-fiber EMG (not needed when RNS is diagnostic)
action_criteria.rationale: RNS already shows a decrement in three muscles with positive AChR antibodies; single-fiber EMG adds no diagnostic information but is not wasteful.

action_criteria.label: Review guidance on the management of generalized myasthenia gravis
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading on management; not a clinical step in the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.

Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not attribute the ptosis and bulbar weakness to diabetic cranial neuropathy or brainstem small-vessel disease before AChR antibody testing and neurophysiology.
required_recommendations: Diagnose late-onset AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis with predominantly bulbar involvement: fatigable asymmetric ptosis with Cogan lid twitch, dysarthria and dysphagia worse in the evening, AChR binding antibody 11.2 nmol/L, 12-16% decrement on RNS, no thymoma on mediastinal CT.
Arrange a formal swallowing assessment before oral intake continues, with diet modification or nasogastric feeding if swallowing is unsafe.
Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three to four times daily, taken 30-60 minutes before meals, titrating to effect up to 60 mg four to five times daily.

Start prednisone in hospital, either low dose (10-20 mg/day increasing by 5-10 mg every 3-7 days) or high dose under inpatient monitoring for steroid-induced worsening, with bone protection, and plan a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT testing) if long-term immunosuppression is needed [Sanders_2016].
Intensify glucose monitoring and adjust diabetes treatment (metformin, add insulin if needed) when prednisone starts: HbA1c is already 8.1%.

Repeat FVC and MIP if bulbar or respiratory symptoms worsen, and give IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days or plasma exchange for impending crisis (FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than -30 cmH2O, weak cough or pooled secretions).

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a disorder of the neuromuscular junction (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
CSF has no role in MG (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025); no CNS or Miller Fisher alternative is raised here.
FDG-PET is not indicated in MG; mediastinal CT covers thymoma screening (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
No cardiac question in this patient; echocardiography does not contribute to the diagnosis of MG.
No palpitations, syncope or arrhythmia; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to the diagnosis of MG.

accepted: AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, late-onset, with concurrent lichen planus (autoimmune background)

differential.key_features: Age, hypertension and diabetes raise it, but the deficits fluctuate with fatigability, there are no long-tract signs, and MRI (if obtained) shows no brainstem lesion.
Late-onset ptosis with dysphagia, but a 20-day course with diurnal fluctuation, Cogan lid twitch, positive AChR antibodies and an RNS decrement are against it.
Type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.1%, but diabetic cranial mononeuropathy is acute and affects one nerve; bilateral fatigable ptosis with bulbar weakness and normal nerve conduction do not fit.
Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes, no post-exercise facilitation, preserved reflexes, no autonomic symptoms and positive AChR antibodies.
No tongue wasting or fasciculations, normal needle EMG, fluctuating course and RNS decrement with positive AChR antibodies.
No exposure to penicillamine, immune checkpoint inhibitors or other implicated drugs.

key_clinical_evidence: Asymmetric fatigable ptosis with Cogan lid twitch, nasal dysarthria and dysphagia progressing to liquids, worse in the evening, with fatigable proximal strength.
AChR binding antibody 11.2 nmol/L with elevated blocking antibody; MuSK negative; thyroid function normal.
RNS: 12-16% decrement in anconeus, trapezius and orbicularis oculi, normal CMAPs, no facilitation, normal nerve conduction and needle EMG.
Ice pack test: left MRD1 improved from 0.5 to 3.0 mm.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma. Here it shows age-appropriate thymic involution; thymectomy is not routinely indicated after 65 without thymoma.
HbA1c 8.1% on metformin: steroid treatment will need closer glucose control.
Lichen planus is a coexisting autoimmune skin disease and does not explain the bulbar weakness.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Lichen planus is a coexisting T-cell mediated skin disease; it does not cause bulbar or ocular weakness, and no paraneoplastic or connective tissue process is suggested.
red_herrings.data_point: Lichen planus on skin exam — considered as possible paraneoplastic or connective tissue disorder
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lichen planus with bulbar dysfunction might suggest a paraneoplastic process or SLE with neurological involvement

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal nerve conduction on the RNS study; diabetes does not cause bilateral fatigable ptosis with bulbar weakness. The HbA1c matters for steroid planning, not for the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Elevated HbA1c (8.1%) suggesting poorly controlled diabetes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Poorly controlled diabetes with peripheral neuropathy could cause mild bulbar dysfunction

sequence_constraints.reason: AChR antibody testing precedes single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative patients or a normal RNS (Jacob 2025).
Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; SFEMG follows when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).

myasthenia gravis.query: myasthenia gravis diagnosis and treatment guidance

results.finding: Consensus guidance recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: In the MGTX trial thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.
results.source: Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522 (MGTX)

myasthenia gravis.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders 2016; update Narayanaswami 2021): AChR antibody testing first, MuSK when AChR antibodies are absent, RNS or single-fiber EMG for electrodiagnostic confirmation, chest CT or MRI in all patients for thymoma. MGTX (Wolfe 2016): thymectomy improved three-year outcomes in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

mri.impression: No acute brainstem lesion. Mild nonspecific periventricular white matter changes. Normal brainstem.

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Fatigable ptosis, bulbar dysfunction; RNS for NMJ assessment

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz trains of 10 stimuli, limb temperature 33 C, at anconeus (radial nerve), trapezius (accessory nerve), and orbicularis oculi (facial nerve)

RESULTS:
  Anconeus: Decrement 14% from 1st to 4th stimulus [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Trapezius: Decrement 16% ABNORMAL
  Orbicularis oculi: Decrement 12% ABNORMAL

MOTOR NERVE CONDUCTION: Normal distal latencies and amplitudes; no evidence of peripheral neuropathy.

SENSORY NERVE CONDUCTION: Normal.

NEEDLE EMG (distal and proximal muscles): Normal insertional activity; no fibrillations, no fasciculations; no myopathic or neuropathic motor unit morphology changes.

POST-EXERCISE (10 s maximal contraction, anconeus): CMAP increment 4%; no facilitation.

IMPRESSION: Abnormal decremental responses at 3 Hz in three muscle groups (anconeus 14%, trapezius 16%, orbicularis 12%). Normal needle EMG and nerve conduction. No post-exercise facilitation. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Decrement of 12-16% at 3 Hz in anconeus, trapezius and orbicularis oculi. 2. Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes and no post-exercise facilitation. 3. Normal nerve conduction and needle EMG. Findings are consistent with a postsynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 69-year-old Indian man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a chronic violaceous pruritic skin eruption on the extremities (diagnosed one year earlier as lichen planus by dermatology) presented to the neurology ward with a 20-day history of mild bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and progressive dysphagia. Dysarthria developed first — a nasal quality to his speech that his wife noticed was more pronounced by evening — followed within 3 days by difficulty swallowing solids that progressed over the next week to difficulty with liquids. He noted that symptoms were consistently and markedly better in the morning upon waking and significantly worsened through the afternoon and evening. He denied diplopia, headache, vertigo, dizziness, shortness of breath, or limb weakness.

He had no recent infections, travel, or significant dietary changes. His family history was unremarkable for neuromuscular disease. On physical examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Dermatologic examination confirmed flat-topped violaceous papules on the flexural surfaces of both lower extremities with overlying hyperpigmented macules — characteristic lichen planus morphology. Neurological examination demonstrated asymmetric bilateral ptosis (left greater than right) without ophthalmoplegia. Gag reflex was severely reduced. Palate elevation was symmetric but weak. Tongue movements were intact with no fasciculations or atrophy. Proximal muscle strength was 5/5 with clinically apparent fatigability on sustained resistance testing. Reflexes were 2+ symmetric. Sensation was intact throughout.

neurological_exam.motor: Proximal limb strength 5/5 with clear fatigability on sustained resistance. No fasciculations.
